Chapter 1 - Introduction
 

Bayes theorem is a basic theorem in probability.

Bayesian statistics uses Bayes theorem to solve statistical problems.

In particular, Bayesian inference fits models to data.

Chapter contents:

  1. Simple motivating example to illustrate the basic idea

  2. Review of Bayes theorem and introduction to general framework of Bayesian statistics

  3. Opinion polling example, illustrating many concepts covered in later chapters

  4. Philosophical interpretations of probability, and their relevance to Bayesian statistics

  5. Advantages and disadvantages of Bayesian statistics

1.1 Motivating medical example

A blood test has been developed for a disease.

Let PP denote the event “tests positive” and DD denote the event “has the disease”.

Let C{}^C denote the complement of an event, so PCP^C is the event “tests negative” etc.

Medical trials have determined that ℙ(P|D)=0.9,ℙ(P|DC)=0.2.\mathbb{P}(P | D) = 0.9, \qquad \mathbb{P}(P | D^C) = 0.2.

We also know that ℙ(D)=0.1\mathbb{P}(D)=0.1 (10% of the population currently have the disease).

Question: Find ℙ(D|P)\mathbb{P}(D | P), the probability that you have the disease if you test positive.

We’re given ℙ(P|D)\mathbb{P}(P | D) and need ℙ(D|P)\mathbb{P}(D | P). So we must reverse the order of conditioning. The mathematical tool to do this is Bayes theorem.

Note: We can view PP and DD as binary random variables: they are either 0 or 1. Most of the course will consider continuous random variables. (But discrete random variable questions are still examinable!)

Medical testing solution

Bayes theorem for events is: ℙ(D|P)=ℙ(P|D)ℙ(D)ℙ(P)\mathbb{P}(D | P) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(P | D) \mathbb{P}(D)}{\mathbb{P}(P)} We aren’t given ℙ(P)\mathbb{P}(P) (probability of testing positive without knowing disease status). But we can derive it using the law of total probability: ℙ(P)=ℙ(P|D)ℙ(D)+ℙ(P|DC)ℙ(DC)\mathbb{P}(P) = \mathbb{P}(P | D) \mathbb{P}(D) + \mathbb{P}(P | D^C) \mathbb{P}(D^C) This gives us another version of Bayes theorem: ℙ(D|P)=ℙ(P|D)ℙ(D)ℙ(P|D)ℙ(D)+ℙ(P|DC)ℙ(DC)\mathbb{P}(D | P) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(P | D) \mathbb{P}(D)}{\mathbb{P}(P | D) \mathbb{P}(D) + \mathbb{P}(P | D^C) \mathbb{P}(D^C)} Substituting in the numerical values gives: ℙ(D|P)=0.9×0.10.9×0.1+0.2×(1−0.1)=0.10.1+0.2=1/3\mathbb{P}(D | P) = \frac{0.9 \times 0.1}{0.9 \times 0.1 + 0.2 \times (1-0.1)} = \frac{0.1}{0.1+0.2} = 1/3

Comment: This is a bit counter-intuitive! We have ℙ(P|D)=0.9\mathbb{P}(P | D) = 0.9: if you have the disease you are very likely to test positive. But we’ve concluded ℙ(D|P)=1/3\mathbb{P}(D | P) = 1/3: if you test positive you are moderately unlikely to have the disease.

To see why consider 100 people. On average 10 have the disease, and 9 of these test positive. On average 90 don’t have the disease, and 18 of these test positive. So 1/3 of positive tests are from people with the disease

So our conclusion is because the disease is relatively unusual and false positive tests are relatively common. Bayes theorem helps us assess the importance of these factors without just relying on intuition.

Generalising this example

In this example we are given:

  • A model describing the probability of various possible outcomes (test outcomes) conditional on some parameters (disease status).

  • Prior information about the parameters (ℙ(D)=0.1\mathbb{P}(D) = 0.1).

  • Data specifying the observed outcome (you have tested positive).

We use Bayes theorem to calculate the probability of parameters given data (ℙ(D|P)\mathbb{P}(D | P)).

We now have two probabilities for the parameters:

  • The prior probability ℙ(D)\mathbb{P}(D): before observing the data.

  • The posterior probability ℙ(D|P)\mathbb{P}(D | P): after seeing data.

Bayesian statistics attempts to generalise this approach. Some immediate difficulties are:

  • How to deal with non-discrete parameters and/or data?

  • What if we don’t have prior information in an exact numerical form?

  • Is it always useful to have the answer in the form of a probability?

We’ll see answers to these and other difficulties throughout the course.

1.2 Bayes theorem and Bayesian framework

We’ve seen Bayes theorem for two events AA and BB: ℙ(B|A)=ℙ(A|B)ℙ(B)ℙ(A)\mathbb{P}(B|A) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(A|B) \mathbb{P}(B)}{\mathbb{P}(A)} We can calculate ℙ(A)\mathbb{P}(A) using the law of total probability: ℙ(A)=ℙ(A|B)ℙ(B)+ℙ(A|Bc)ℙ(Bc)\mathbb{P}(A) = \mathbb{P}(A|B)\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(A|B^c)\mathbb{P}(B^c) We’ll mostly use a version of Bayes theorem for continuous random variables. Given continuous random variables XX and YY, with conditional density f(x|y)f(x|y) and marginal density π(y)\pi(y), the conditional density of yy given xx is π(y|x)=f(x|y)π(y)m(x)wherem(x)=∫y∈𝒴f(x|y)π(y)dy\begin{aligned} \pi(y|x) & = \frac{f(x|y)\pi(y)}{m(x)} \\ \text{where} \qquad m(x) & = \int_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} f(x|y)\pi(y) \mathrm{d}y \end{aligned} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is the support of YY (that is, the set of possible values of yy).

In fact the same formula works if XX is discrete. In this case f(x|y)=ℙ(X=x|y)f(x|y) = \mathbb{P}(X=x | y). For example, we could have X∼Binomial(100,y)X \sim \text{Binomial}(100, y) with support 𝒴=[0,1]\mathcal{Y} = [0,1].

It’s common to write y∈[0,1]y \in [0,1] as a quick way to give the support.

Brief history of Bayesian Statistics (not examinable!)

The Reverend Thomas Bayes (1701-1761) discovered Bayes theorem – sometimes written with an apostrophe: “Bayes’ theorem”.

There is only one known portrait of Thomas Bayes, and there is some debate whether it is actually of him!

Bayes theorem was introduced in “An essay towards solving a problem in the doctrine of chances”. This was published posthumously in 1763 by his friend Richard Price who edited the work and added an introduction.

Pierre Simon de Laplace (1749-1827) independently rediscovered Bayes theorem, and introduced many of the concepts that are now the basis of Bayesian statistics.

Bayesian statistics became unpopular in the early/mid 1900s (with frequentist approaches preferred instead). Interest has now revived due to further mathematical/philosophical support, and to powerful new computational methods developed in the 1990s onwards.

The Bayesian Framework: parameters

We now introduce the general setting for Bayesian inference.

Let θ∈Θ\theta \in \Theta be the parameters of interest.

The parameter space is Θ\Theta. We usually assume Θ⊆ℝd\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d. So θ\theta is a vector of dd real-valued parameters.

We treat the parameters as a random variable (discussion later!) We assume it has a prior distribution. When θ\theta is continuous this is defined by its prior density π(θ)\pi(\theta).

Remarks

  • Often we have a prior of the form π(θ)=π1(θ1)π2(θ2)…πd(θd)\pi(\theta) = \pi_1(\theta_1) \pi_2(\theta_2) \ldots \pi_d(\theta_d) where Θ=ℝd\Theta = \mathbb{R}^d and θi∈Θi=ℝ\theta_i \in \Theta_i = \mathbb{R}. That is, the parameters are independent under the prior distribution. In this case we can make statements like “πi(θi)\pi_i(\theta_i) is the prior for θi\theta_i”.

  • Parameters are often represented by Greek letters λ,θ\lambda, \theta etc.
    These letters are used to represent both the random variable – e.g. θ∼𝒰(0,1)\theta \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1) – and its realisation – e.g. θ=0.1\theta = 0.1. The distinction should be clear from the context. (Note the capital Greek letter Θ\Theta is already used for the parameter space!)

The Bayesian Framework: observations

Let X∈𝒳X \in \mathcal{X} be the observable data. This is also treated as a random variable. A realisation of XX is denoted xx.

The observation space is 𝒳\mathcal{X}. We usually assume 𝒳⊆ℝk\mathcal{X}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^k. So xx is a vector of kk observations.

We introduce a parametric probability model {f(x|θ),θ∈Θ}\{f(x|\theta),\,\theta\in\Theta\}. This defines a probability distribution for xx for any choice of θ\theta. For continuous data, f(x|θ)f(x|\theta) is a probability density function. For discrete data, f(x|θ)f(x|\theta) is a probability mass function. In either case we call f(x|θ)f(x|\theta) the likelihood function.

Remark

Observable quantities are usually represented by Roman letters x,yx, y etc. As usual, we generally use capital letters (like XX) for random variables and lower case letters (like xx) for their realisations.

Binomial example (discrete data)

An opinion poll asks 10 students if they prefer maths or statistics.

Let xx be the number who prefer maths. Then the observation space is 𝒳={0,1,2,…,10}.\mathcal{X} = \{ 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 10 \}.

Let θ\theta be the probability someone prefers maths. Then θ∈Θ=[0,1]\theta \in \Theta = [0,1]. We could assume a uniform prior θ∼𝒰(0,1)\theta \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1), so π(θ)=1\pi(\theta) = 1 for θ∈Θ\theta \in \Theta.

Suppose we use a Binomial model for the outcome: X∼Bin(10,θ)X \sim \text{Bin}(10, \theta). Then our likelihood is f(x|θ)=(10x)θx(1−θ)10−x.f(x|\theta) = \binom{10}{x} \theta^x (1-\theta)^{10-x}.

Remark

Here we define π(θ)\pi(\theta) and f(x|θ)f(x | \theta) only for θ∈Θ=[0,1]\theta \in \Theta = [0,1]. The formulae will not necessarily make sense for other θ\theta values.

We’ll continue this example in Section 1.3.

Normal example (continuous data)

Let xx be a blood pressure measurement and θ\theta be the true blood pressure.

For simplicity let’s assume x∈𝒳=ℝx \in \mathcal{X} = \mathbb{R} and θ∈Θ=ℝ\theta \in \Theta = \mathbb{R}.

Let’s assume a Normal prior distribution, θ∼𝒩1(90,102)\theta \sim \mathcal{N}_1(90, 10^2). Then π(θ)=12π10exp⁡(−1200[θ−90]2).\pi(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi} 10} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{200}[\theta - 90]^2 \right).

Let’s assume X=θ+ϵX = \theta + \epsilon where ϵ∼𝒩1(0,32)\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}_1(0, 3^2) is measurement error. Then X|θ∼𝒩1(θ,32)X | \theta \sim \mathcal{N}_1(\theta, 3^2) and the likelihood is f(x|θ)=12π3exp⁡(−118[x−θ]2).f(x | \theta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi} 3} \exp \left( -\frac{1}{18}[x - \theta]^2 \right).

Remarks

  • Later we sometimes use the notation 𝒩d\mathcal{N}_d for a dd-dimensional normal distribution. The subscript is dropped where the dimension is clear (or not important).

  • This model allows negative blood pressure, which is not very realistic! However the probability of negative values is incredibly small.

Medical testing example

We can put the medical testing example into this framework as follows.

The parameter is θ∈Θ={D,DC}\theta \in \Theta = \{ D, D^C \} (disease status). The prior distribution is given by ℙ(θ=D)=0.1ℙ(θ=DC)=0.9.\mathbb{P}(\theta = D) = 0.1 \qquad \mathbb{P}(\theta = D^C) = 0.9.

The outcome is X∈𝒳={P,PC}X \in \mathcal{X} = \{ P, P^C \}. Our likelihood is given by f(X=P|θ=D)=0.9f(X=PC|θ=D)=0.1f(X=P|θ=DC)=0.2f(X=PC|θ=DC)=0.8.\begin{aligned} f(X=P | \theta=D) & = 0.9 \\ f(X=P^C | \theta=D) & = 0.1 \\ f(X=P | \theta=D^C) & = 0.2 \\ f(X=P^C | \theta=D^C) & = 0.8. \end{aligned}

Remark

This example has discrete data and discrete parameters.

Types of model

Here we introduce some classes of model and their likelihoods. Let x1,…,xnx_1,\dots,x_n be nn observations in 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_1, so that x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_1,\dots,x_n) and 𝒳=𝒳1n\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_1^n.

  • Independent and identically distributed (IID): Here f(x|θ)=∏k=1nf̃(xk|θ)f(x|\theta)=\prod_{k=1}^n\tilde{f}(x_k|\theta) where {f̃(⋅|θ),θ∈Θ}\{\tilde{f}(\cdot|\theta),\,\theta\in\Theta\} is a parametric model for x1x_1.

  • Time series: The observations now assumed to be dependent, f(x|θ)=f̃1(x1|θ)∏t=2nf̃t(xt|x1,…,xt−1,θ)f(x|\theta)=\tilde{f}_1(x_1|\theta)\prod_{t=2}^n\tilde{f}_t(x_t|x_1,\dots, x_{t-1},\theta) where {f̃1(⋅|θ),θ∈Θ⊆ℝd}\{\tilde{f}_1(\cdot|\theta),\,\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\} is a parametric model for x1x_1 and {f̃t(⋅|x1,…,xt−1,θ),θ∈Θ}\{\tilde{f}_t(\cdot|x_1,\dots, x_{t-1},\theta),\,\theta\in\Theta\} is a parametric model for xtx_t given x1,…,xt−1x_1,\dots,x_{t-1}.

Maximum likelihood and Frequentist Methods

Bayesian methods are one framework for statistics.

Another popular framework is frequentist methods. Particularly relevant is maximum likelihood.

Maximum likelihood uses a similar setting to Bayesian statistics. But the parameters are not treated as random variables, and a prior distribution is not required.

Maximum likelihood estimates the parameters as θ̂=argmax⁡θ∈Θf(x|θ)\hat{\theta} = \mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{\theta \in \Theta} f(x|\theta) where xx is the observed data. So θ̂\hat{\theta} is the parameter vector which maximises the likelihood.

Parameter uncertainty is described using confidence intervals.

Remark:

There can be issues with existence and uniqueness of θ̂\hat{\theta}, but we won’t go into the details here.

The Bayesian Framework: posterior

Bayesian inference aims to find the posterior distribution for the parameters conditional on the data. This can then be used to find parameter estimates and intervals (details later).

When θ\theta is continuous, Bayes theorem gives that the posterior density is: π(θ|x)=π(θ)f(x|θ)m(x).\pi(\theta | x ) = \frac{\pi(\theta) f(x|\theta)} { m(x) }. where xx is the observed data and m(x)=∫Θf(x|θ)π(θ)dθm(x)=\int_{\Theta}f(x|\theta)\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta is called the evidence.

It’s sometimes useful to simplify Bayes theorem to π(θ|x)∝π(θ)f(x|θ).\pi(\theta | x ) \propto \pi(\theta) f(x|\theta). In words: “posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood”. This avoids the m(x)m(x) term which is often hard to calculate.

Remarks

The name ‘evidence’ for m(x)m(x) becomes relevant in Chapter 7 on model choice. It can be used to judge how much the data supports different models.

We can also view m(x)m(x) as:

  • The marginal density of xx.

  • The normalising constant in Bayes theorem for a particular choice of xx.

Proportionality method

Many mathematical derivations in Bayesian statistics (including the example on the next pages) are simplified by using the following result about proportionality.

Theorem 1.1. Suppose p(θ),q(θ)p(\theta), q(\theta) are two probability density functions for θ∈Θ⊆ℝd\theta \in \Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d, and q(θ)∝p(θ).q(\theta) \propto p(\theta). Then q(θ)=p(θ)q(\theta) = p(\theta).

Proof

Since q(θ)∝p(θ)q(\theta) \propto p(\theta), there exists a constant cc such that q(θ)=cp(θ).q(\theta) = c p(\theta). Integrating gives ∫Θq(θ)dθ=c∫Θp(θ)dθ.\int_{\Theta} q(\theta) \mathrm{d}\theta = c \int_{\Theta} p(\theta) \mathrm{d}\theta. Both integrals equal one (since pp and qq are probability density functions).

So c=1c=1 and q(θ)=p(θ)q(\theta) = p(\theta).

1.3 Polling example

The following simple example illustrates many concepts covered later in the course.

An opinion poll asks nn people whether they prefer maths or statistics. Let xx be the number who prefer maths, and θ\theta be the probability that a randomly selected person prefers maths. We have n=10n=10 and x=8x=8. Perform a Bayesian analysis to infer θ\theta.

Here the probability model is X∼Binomial(n,θ)X \sim \text{Binomial}(n,\theta) (under standard assumptions i.e. poll responses are iid – independent and identically distributed).

So the likelihood is f(x|θ)=(nx)θx(1−θ)n−xf(x|\theta) = \binom{n}{x} \theta^x (1-\theta)^{n-x} for θ∈Θ=[0,1]\theta \in \Theta = [0,1].

It’s easy to derive (see Problem 1.4) that this is maximised by θ̂=x/n=0.8\hat{\theta}=x/n=0.8, which is the maximum likelihood estimate. We will compare this to Bayesian results.

For a Bayesian analysis, we also need a prior distribution for θ\theta. We’d like to base this on prior knowledge. But the question doesn’t give us any! We can try to express this prior ignorance by essentially assuming all θ\theta values in Θ\Theta are equally likely. So we take π(θ)=1\pi(\theta) = 1 for θ∈[0,1]\theta \in [0,1] i.e. a 𝒰(0,1)\mathcal{U}(0,1) prior. This is an example of an objective prior: see Chapter 2 for more.

Note: As before, we only consider θ∈Θ=[0,1]\theta \in \Theta = [0,1]. The formulae derived will not necessarily apply or make sense for other θ\theta values.

Polling example: posterior calculation

We now have a prior and likelihood: π(θ)=1f(x|θ)=(nx)θx(1−θ)n−x.\begin{aligned} \pi(\theta) & = 1 \\ f(x|\theta) & = \binom{n}{x} \theta^x (1-\theta)^{n-x}. \end{aligned} We can combine these using Bayes’ theorem to find the posterior density.

We will now use proportionality, ignoring factors not involving θ\theta: π(θ|x)=π(θ)f(x|θ)m(x)∝π(θ)f(x|θ)∝θx(1−θ)n−x\begin{aligned} \pi(\theta | x) & = \frac{\pi(\theta) f(x | \theta)}{m(x)} \\ & \propto \pi(\theta) f(x | \theta) \\ & \propto \theta^x (1-\theta)^{n-x} \end{aligned} Compare this to a Beta(a,b)\text{Beta}(a,b) density, q(θ;a,b)=Γ(a+b)Γ(a)Γ(b)θa−1(1−θ)b−1.q(\theta; a, b) = \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \theta^{a-1} (1-\theta)^{b-1}. We see π(θ|x)∝q(θ;x+1,n+1−x)\pi(\theta | x) \propto q(\theta; x+1, n+1-x). By Theorem 1.1 these densities are equal. So the posterior distribution is Beta(x+1,n+1−x)\text{Beta}(x+1, n+1-x).

For our values x=8,n=10x=8, n=10, we get Beta(9,3)\text{Beta}(9, 3).

In fact the prior is also a Beta distribution: Beta(1,1)\text{Beta}(1,1) gives the same density as 𝒰(0,1)\mathcal{U}(0,1). This is an example of a conjugate prior, which produces a posterior in the same family of distributions: see Chapter 2 for more.

Remark:

The proportionality method allowed us to avoid calculating m(x)m(x) or any Γ\Gamma terms.

Polling example: summaries

How can we summarise our Beta(9,3)\text{Beta}(9, 3) posterior distribution usefully? One approach is to plot its density:

We’d also like a point estimate of the single “best” θ\theta value. Some options are:

  • The posterior expectation 𝔼[θ|x]=∫Θθπ(θ|x)dθ\mathbb{E}[\theta | x] = \int_\Theta \theta \pi(\theta | x) \mathrm{d}\theta

  • The posterior median θm such that ∫−∞θmπ(θ|x)dθ=0.5\theta_m \text{ such that } \int_{-\infty}^{\theta_m} \pi(\theta | x) \mathrm{d}\theta = 0.5

  • The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate argmax⁡θ∈Θπ(θ|x)\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{\theta \in \Theta} \pi(\theta | x)

Chapter 5 discusses theoretical support for these estimates.

Polling example: summaries continued

Let’s calculate the posterior expectation for the polling example.

A Beta(a,b)\text{Beta}(a,b) random variable has expectation aa+b\frac{a}{a+b}. So our Beta(x+1,n+1−x)\text{Beta}(x+1, n+1-x) posterior has expectation x+1n+2=9/12=0.75\frac{x+1}{n+2} = 9/12 = 0.75.

This is smaller than the MLE which equals x/n=0.8x/n = 0.8.

In fact it’s a weighted average of the MLE and the prior expectation of 0.5: 𝔼[θ|x]=λθ̂+(1−λ)𝔼[θ]\mathbb{E}[\theta | x] = \lambda \hat{\theta} + (1-\lambda) \mathbb{E}[\theta] (for some λ∈[0,1]\lambda \in [0,1] depending on xx and nn). See Problem 1.4 for more details and proof.

For large nn, 𝔼[θ|x]→θ̂\mathbb{E}[\theta | x] \to \hat{\theta}: the large amount of data outweighs the prior information. Chapter 8 proves general convergence results along these lines.

Polling example: JAGS

Bayesian calculations with a conjugate prior can be fairly simple. However for most problems there is no conjugate prior, and computer software is needed, such as JAGS (see Chapter 4).

JAGS outputs a sample of θ\theta values from the posterior. These can be used to approximate various summaries e.g. density plot, posterior expectation. This approach is known as Monte Carlo.

The JAGS code for this example is short and similar to the mathematical description:

library(jagsUI)
modelstring="
model{
theta dunif(0,1)
x dbinom(theta,n)
}
"
bin_data=list(x=15,n=20)
set.seed(1)
out=jags(
data=bin_data,
parameters.to.save=c("theta"),
model.file=textConnection(modelstring),
n.chains=4,
n.iter=1000,
DIC=FALSE
)
out
plot(out)
